note: Acts on the 2026-08-17 complexity audit (FINDINGS-2026-08-17-complexity-audit.md, four parallel auditors over docs / CLI-UI-MCP / core library / governance). Batch 1 is the pure-win subset — fixes with no policy or behaviour tradeoff. Shipped: a friendly error when a global --db/--ledger/--json is placed after the subcommand (cli.py _HintingParser); default verbs for the single-choice 'decision'/'db' subcommands; a note when --json is dropped for ui/serve; a RuntimeWarning when abs_tol/pct_tol are passed to a non-numeric matcher (answer.py), matching how nestor serve already refuses it; engine.translate probed by inspect.signature instead of except-TypeError (cascade._accepted_kwargs) so a real bug inside a custom engine is no longer swallowed; the Storage docstring corrected from 'six' optional capabilities to nine, with a drift test; a shared NestorError base for the fifteen policy-refusal exceptions. Draft. tests/test_complexity_audit_batch1.py (26 tests); full suite 1410 passed (one pre-existing environmental version-metadata flake, passes in isolation). Deferred with reasons: Curator.list rename (breaks a public method) and home_init's os.environ mutation (load-bearing given home_paths' env-based resolution — needs a root-threading change, not a safe pure-win).

decisions.question: The refusal exceptions have no common base — a host turning a policy refusal into an HTTP 409 must import a dozen names from six modules and will miss the next one. Give them a base — but which exceptions, and what base?
decisions.commitment: A new NestorError(RuntimeError) that the fifteen RuntimeError-based refusals subclass (memory's four seal guards, the three keyring errors, the three sqlite store errors, curator, ledger, signing, config, home_paths). It stays a RuntimeError, so every existing `except RuntimeError` still catches them. The two ValueError-based errors -- PersonaError and BundleError -- are left out: a malformed bundle or persona spec is bad input, not a policy refusal, and reparenting them under RuntimeError would change which except clause catches them. A drift test pins that every listed refusal subclasses the base.
decisions.why: The base is only worth adding if it can be caught generically AND does not silently change existing catches. Subclassing RuntimeError satisfies both -- it widens what you can catch (NestorError) without narrowing what you already catch (RuntimeError). Folding the ValueError pair in would have required either multiple inheritance or flipping their base, and both change observable behaviour for a caller who catches ValueError today; the format/refusal distinction is real and worth keeping, so the base tracks refusals only.
decisions.doors_closed: A base that changes an exception's existing MRO (breaks `except ValueError`/`except RuntimeError` call sites). A 'catch-all' that also swallows format/validation errors, erasing the input-vs-refusal distinction.

decisions.question: A draft engine's translate() may accept store=/matcher=, one, or neither. The old probe called with both and caught TypeError to retry with fewer args. What replaces it?
decisions.commitment: inspect.signature(engine.translate) decides which of store=/matcher= the callable actually accepts (everything if it takes **kwargs, or if it cannot be introspected -- the old permissive fallback). The engine is then called exactly once with the accepted kwargs.
decisions.why: Catching TypeError to detect a signature cannot tell 'this engine does not accept matcher=' from a genuine TypeError raised inside the engine body -- the latter was silently reinterpreted as a signature mismatch and the call retried with fewer args, running side effects (e.g. a second draft-API call) and burying the real bug. Reading the signature answers the same question without catching an exception the engine meant to raise, so a real engine bug now surfaces instead of vanishing.
decisions.doors_closed: Using exception handling as signature detection (swallows unrelated TypeErrors; double side effects on retry).
